Pejerrey Odontesthes argentinensis is a euryhaline atherinopsid inhabiting coastal and estuarine environments of the southwestern Atlantic, where it supports both commercial and recreational fisheries. Field surveys along the Argentine coast indicate that individuals can attain a maximum total length of 42.1 centimeters [Li = 42.1 centimeters], a value derived from extensive gillnet sampling across multiple seasons. This ultimate size is accompanied by an estimated ultimate wet weight of 480 grams [Wwi = 480 grams], following the allometric relationship observed for the species, which closely matches the mass-length scaling documented in related silversides. The age structure of captured specimens suggests that such maximum dimensions are achieved only after several years of sustained somatic growth.

Sexual maturation in this species is a gradual process linked to seasonal fat accumulation, with the total length at puberty recorded at 16.1 centimeters [Lp = 16.1 centimeters]. This value was established through histological examination of gonadal tissue combined with length-frequency data collected during the winter months, a period when individuals prioritise reserve storage. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated from the same series of specimens, is 26 grams [Wwp = 26 grams], reflecting the body condition typical of fish that have completed their first full year of growth. Individuals below this size are rarely observed with developing gonads, reinforcing the hypothesis that a minimum somatic threshold must be reached before reproductive investment begins.

Reproductive output in Odontesthes argentinensis has been quantified through controlled laboratory experiments at a constant temperature of 15.9 °C [T = 15.9 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, females with total lengths ranging from 21.2 to 34.2 centimeters, and a mean length of 27.5 centimeters, produce approximately 27 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 27 eggs per spawning event], and they typically spawn once per day [F_R_i = spawn once per day]. This high-frequency reproductive strategy maximises the number of offspring produced over the breeding season. The daily egg production rate at this temperature corresponds to about 27 eggs per day, a rate considerably higher than that observed in cooler environments, where spawning intervals lengthen appreciably.

The early life stages of this species begin with a remarkably small neonate; newly hatched larvae weigh just 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams]. This minute wet weight at birth reflects the high fecundity strategy typical of atherinopsids, where small egg size enables the production of numerous offspring over an extended spawning season. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for several days before the onset of exogenous feeding. The rapid depletion of these reserves underscores the importance of timely first feeding in rearing environments, as larvae that fail to locate suitable prey within a critical window experience high mortality.

Longevity records for wild populations of Odontesthes argentinensis indicate a maximum lifespan of 7 years [am = 7 years] when evaluated at an ambient temperature of 15.9 °C [T = 15.9 °C]. This estimate originates from otolith-based age determination of individuals captured across a latitudinal gradient, demonstrating that individuals inhabiting cooler waters tend to live longer than their counterparts in warmer regions. The species exhibits an iteroparous reproductive schedule consistent with other Atherinopsidae, where adult females spawn daily during the breeding season, a strategy that distributes reproductive effort across multiple cohorts and buffers against stochastic environmental variation in coastal habitats. Comparative data from other atherinopsid genera suggest that a seven-year lifespan is relatively long for a fish of this body size, likely linked to its slow juvenile growth and the energetic demands of its high-frequency spawning strategy.
